title: Trump admin agrees to consider golf plan changes after key agency punts on approval | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Faced with overwhelmingly negative public feedback, the Trump administration opened the door to considering design changes for redeveloping a beloved municipal recreational land into the championship golf course the president desires.

The move comes after a key agency that oversees federal design and building changes in Washington, DC, declined to approve the plans on Thursday, despite signals from the administration that it wanted to move quickly on President Donald Trump’s construction projects.

However, the chair of the Commission of Fine Arts (CFA) – whose members are mostly Trump-appointed allies – said the administration should “sharpen their pencils” and come back with a new design that keeps the peninsula available to more people, and honors, rather than eliminates, many of the current features of the land, like the Ohio Driveway that local runners and cyclists use, as well as a mini-golf greenway frequented by families.

The plans the administration presented Thursday for the first time would wipe out several recreational uses of the land and essentially only allows for one, 36-hole championship course instead.

The Department of Interior agreed to consider changes, but did not commit to coming back with a completely new proposal.

The administration will present the plans to the commission at their next meeting in January. It is possible that no changes are made, but opponents of the project said they were pleasantly surprised and satisfied that the administration has agreed to at least consider alterations in the interim.

The agency reported receiving over 700 comments about the project, overwhelmingly in opposition. Only three, they said, were in support of the current plans.

Many opponents spoke up at the CFA meeting, with publiccomments that spanned over an hour highlighting their feelings of what would be lost if the land was converted from a multi-use space to only housing a golf course.

“I implore you, don’t move forward with this,” Alexander Howell, a DC resident, told the CFA. “Show the public that your sense of design encompasses all of us, all of our needs.”

A member of a local bike group, who uses the Ohio Driveway loop for training, said, “this plan is so half baked and ineffective and doesn’t take into account millions of the people who use it and love it every year.”

Ultimately, the CFA punted on approval.

The unexpected setback also comes as the golf course, like many other Trump projects, is ensnared in legal battles that have dealt setbacks to their progress.

Though hints of what changes were planned for the golf course have dribbled out in previous months, the plans that were presented to the CFA first surfaced officially in a court hearing last Friday in a case aimed at stopping the redevelopment.

Following that hearing, US District Judge Ana C. Reyes said the administration’s push to revamp East Potomac Golf Links likely violated environmental law and ran afoul of procedural guardrails for executive-branch actions.

She issued a temporary order halting work on Saturday, and has previously accused government attorneys of misleading her.

The Justice Department has unsuccessfully tried to remove her from the case, brought by preservationists and golfers seeking to stop the redevelopment arguing that changing the course would run afoul of federal environmental regulations and diminish public access.

Trump, an avid golfer, first publicly proposed the idea of taking over and expanding the municipal golf course in May and was soon thereafter seen touring the grounds with Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Tom Fazio, a well-known golf designer who worked on several of Trump’s private courses.
